title: Drinks and memories
hook: No shop sells the drinks you grew up with. Can you put those memories in a bottle and make money?

profit.label: Cash
profit.hint: The money you have left to keep going

future.label: Brand
future.hint: How many people know your drinks, and how much they love them

intro.text: You and three partners run a small drinks company. Your energy drink, Tzinga, costs ₹25, much less than the biggest energy drink at ₹95. But you have little money left, and it must last until you find a drink that sells well.

idea.text: One partner's mother makes aam panna, a raw mango drink, and he often brings it to work. The team wants more, so you look in shops but find none. No shop sells aam panna, jaljeera, a cumin drink, or the other drinks you grew up with.

d1.title: Where to spend your money
d1.setup: Tzinga is growing, but only one kind of buyer wants energy drinks, and only at certain times. Many more people buy fruit juice, and shops don't sell the old drinks made at home. You have enough money to try one idea, but your team cannot agree.
d1.question: Where do you put your money?
d1.advisor: Tzinga already sells. Why bet our money on a drink no shop has ever sold?

options.label: Spend more on Tzinga. It already sells, but only to a few buyers.
options.outcome: Tzinga sells a little more, but the buyers are still the same small group. Big brands spend far more than you on ads. A year later, sales stop growing, and you still haven't tried the aam panna idea.
options.why: Remember: a bad fix people already use proves the pain is real. Here, mothers made these drinks at home because shops didn't sell them. Making them took time, but people still did it. Tzinga had buyers, but the drinks made at home showed that more people wanted something shops didn't sell.
options.better: Sell the drinks people grew up with but couldn't find in shops.
options.takeaway: In 2012 you spent more on the drink you already sold. But more people wanted drinks that shops didn't sell.

options.label: Bottle home drinks like aam panna. They're new, and Tzinga gets less.
options.outcome: You start making Indian home drinks like aam panna and jaljeera. They have no fizz, no preservatives (chemicals that keep drinks fresh) and no added colours. You call them Paper Boat, after the paper boats children float in the monsoon rain.
options.why: Remember: a bad fix people already use proves the pain is real. Here, mothers made these drinks at home because shops didn't sell them. It took time, but they still made them. That showed people wanted these drinks.
options.takeaway: In 2012 you sold drinks people loved but couldn't buy. Good ideas can come from things people already want.

options.label: Sell fruit juices. Many people buy them, but big brands already sell them.
options.outcome: Your mango and orange juices reach shops, but many other juices look just like yours. Shops ask for big discounts before they will sell your juice. After a year, you are still a small brand among many others.
options.why: Remember: a bad fix people already use proves the pain is real. People didn't need to make mango juice at home because shops already sold it. But they still made drinks like aam panna at home because shops didn't sell them.
options.better: Sell the drinks people grew up with but couldn't find in shops.
options.takeaway: In 2012 you entered a market with many brands. Finding something people want but cannot buy can be better than selling what many shops already have.

d2.title: How will you pack the drink?

setup.text: You have lost a year, and Tzinga has stopped growing. So you try the aam panna idea and call it Paper Boat, after the paper boats children float in the rain. Now you must choose a pack, and every pack adds to the cost of your drink.

Your juices are not selling well, so you try drinks no shop sells: aam panna and jaljeera. You call them Paper Boat, after the paper boats children float in the rain. Now you must choose a pack, and every pack adds to the cost of your drink.
Your drinks are ready, but now you need a pack. Every pack adds to your cost. You want the drink to remind people of home and feel special, not like a cheap cola. It must also travel across India.

d2.question: What kind of pack will you use?
d2.advisor: Big juice brands use cartons. Shops know how to keep them on shelves, and buyers already trust them.

options.label: Use a paper-look pouch. It costs less, but buyers may not trust it.
options.outcome: You choose a 250 ml pouch that stands on the shelf and looks like paper. It costs less than a carton, so you keep more money from every sale. It also looks different from other drinks.
options.why: Remember: price minus stock cost isn't profit. Count every hidden cost. The pack adds to the cost of each drink. A cheaper pack left you more money from every sale, and it also looked different on the shelf.
options.takeaway: In 2013 you chose a pack that cost less and looked different. Saving a little on every pack can save a lot of money.

options.label: Use juice cartons. Buyers trust them, but they cost more.
options.outcome: Your drinks look neat and safe on the shelf, but each carton costs more and leaves you less money from every sale. You must charge more than the juices beside them to make money, so many buyers walk past.
options.why: Remember: price minus stock cost isn't profit. Count every hidden cost. The pack adds to the cost of each drink. Costly cartons left you less money from every sale, so you had less money to grow.
options.better: Use a cheaper pack, like a pouch, and make it look special.
options.takeaway: In 2013 you chose a costly pack. Even a few extra rupees on every pack can cost your business a lot.

options.label: Use plastic bottles. They're cheap and strong, but look ordinary.
options.outcome: The bottles are cheap and strong, but your aam panna looks like another soft drink on the shelf. Buyers cannot see how it is different from colas unless they stop and read the label.
options.why: Remember: price minus stock cost isn't profit. Count every hidden cost. The bottle kept the pack cost low, so you still made money on each sale. But the pack didn't show buyers why your drink was special.
options.better: Use a pack that costs less and looks different, like a paper-look pouch.
options.takeaway: In 2013 you saved money on the pack, but your drink looked like all the others.

d3.title: What will you write on the pack?
d3.setup: You have almost no money for ads, so most people will first see your drink on a shop shelf. Each pack has a small space where you can print anything you want.
d3.question: What do you print on the pack?
d3.advisor: Buyers read packs to know what they're buying. Tell them clearly what's inside, and be honest.

options.label: Print the name and what's inside. It's clear, but looks ordinary.
options.outcome: The packs look neat, and buyers can see there is no fizz and nothing artificial. But nothing on the pack makes them smile or want to buy another one.
options.why: Remember: people pick brands they remember, and a voice they enjoy helps. Clear facts helped, but every juice pack has facts. Your pack gave people no reason to remember your brand.
options.better: Add a short, warm story or a small joke to each pack, so people enjoy reading it.
options.takeaway: In 2013 you kept the pack simple. Clear facts are useful, but they may not help people remember your brand.

options.label: Print a film star's photo. People know them, but fees are high.
options.outcome: You spend most of your money for the year paying the film star. People notice the packs, but they remember the star, not your drink. When the deal ends, you have nothing special of your own.
options.why: Remember: people pick brands they remember, and a voice they enjoy helps. People remembered the star, not your drink. You paid a lot to use someone else's fame instead of giving your brand its own voice.
options.better: Write a short, warm story on each pack, so people remember the drink itself.
options.takeaway: In 2013 you paid to use a film star's face. Your brand needs something people can remember on its own.

options.label: Print a childhood story. It feels warm, but leaves less space for facts.
options.outcome: Each pack tells a short childhood story, like climbing mango trees. There is also a small joke at the bottom for anyone who reads it. Your drink now has its own way of talking to people.
options.why: Remember: people pick brands they remember, and a voice they enjoy helps. The pack was your only ad, so you gave people something they would enjoy reading. The warm stories made people feel close to your brand and remember it.
options.takeaway: In 2013 you gave every pack a story. When people enjoy reading your pack, it can also work as an ad.

d4.title: How will people try it?
d4.setup: Your drinks are ready, but nobody has bought jaljeera in a pack before. Small shops don't want to use shelf space for a drink their buyers haven't asked for. You have enough money to try one big idea.
d4.question: How do you get people to try it?
d4.advisor: Without ads, nobody will know about us. One good TV ad could make shops want our drinks in a month.

options.label: Run TV ads first. Many people learn your name, but ads cost a lot.
options.outcome: People like your ads, and many across India hear your name. But they still cannot find the drink in their local shops. You are running out of money, so by the end of the year you must spend less to save cash.
options.why: Remember: take the risk off the buyer. Shops were afraid they would be left with drinks they couldn't sell. Ads made people want to try the drinks, but shops still had that risk. So people couldn't find the drink easily.
options.better: Let shops return packs they cannot sell, and sell the drink in places where people already go. Run ads later.
options.takeaway: In 2013 you paid for ads before enough shops sold the drink. Help people find and try it first.

options.label: Skip ads and refund unsold packs. Shops feel safer, but returns cost you.

outcome.text: In February 2013 you quietly sell the drinks in 500 big stores in four cities, with no ads. They sell so fast that you decide to make more. In August you launch in Delhi and Bengaluru. Flights and office canteens serve your drinks, and shops can return unsold packs for a full refund.
You quietly sell the drinks in big stores with no ads, and they sell faster than you hoped. Flights and office canteens serve your drinks. Shops can also return unsold packs for a full refund.

options.why: Remember: take the risk off the buyer. Your first buyers were the shops. They were afraid of being left with drinks they couldn't sell. A full refund on unsold packs removed that fear, and the drinks sold well.
options.takeaway: In 2013 you let people try the drink before running ads. Make it easier for shops to sell something new.

options.label: Charge the same as cola. More people try it, but you earn less.
options.outcome: Many people try the drink, but you now lose money on every pack. The more you sell, the faster you run out of cash. Your drink also starts to look like an ordinary cola, and raising the price later is hard.
options.why: Remember: take the risk off the buyer. Shops were afraid of being left with drinks they couldn't sell. Price wasn't the problem. Charging the same as cola made you lose money on every pack and made your special drink look ordinary.
options.better: Keep your price, but let shops return packs they cannot sell.
options.takeaway: In 2013 you cut the price to get more people to try your drink. Raising it later was hard, and the drink looked ordinary.

text.text: Through 2014 you still run no TV or newspaper ads. You share drawings of childhood memories on Facebook, and the packs served on flights become your best ads. Late in 2014, you put post boxes in office canteens so people can send letters to their parents, and you pay to send them.
Through 2014 you spend less to save money after paying for ads. People already know your name, and more shops slowly start selling your drinks. At last, people who saw the ads can find them.
Through 2014 you slowly raise your price again, and some people who bought the cheaper drink stop buying it. Those who stay like the taste, but you have even less money left.

d5.title: What makes your drink special?

setup.text: It's 2015. Your earlier ads made your brand known, and now investors will pay for a bigger TV ad. Your drinks have no preservatives, no added colours and no fizz. Other brands sell fruit juice and cola. Some experts say young buyers and people in the South won't care about childhood memories.

It's 2015. Money is tight, but investors will pay for one TV ad if it works. Your drinks have no preservatives, no added colours and no fizz. Other brands sell fruit juice and cola. Some experts say young buyers and people in the South won't care about childhood memories.

It's 2015, and you finally have money for TV ads. Your drinks have no preservatives, no added colours and no fizz. Other brands sell fruit juice and cola. Some experts say young buyers and people in the South won't care about childhood memories.

d5.question: What should your first big ad say?
d5.advisor: Many buyers care about health. Tell them clearly what's inside your drink and what you've left out.

options.label: Show what's not inside. It's honest, but every juice says much the same.
options.outcome: Your ads show fresh fruit and clearly tell people what is not in the drink. People like that, but the ad looks like other juice ads on TV. Few remember which brand it was for, so sales grow slowly.
options.why: Remember: sell what you stand for, not just specs. A list of what's inside tells people about the product. Other juice brands can say much the same, so your ad didn't give people anything special to remember.
options.takeaway: In 2015 you told people what was inside. Other brands can do that too, so tell people what makes yours special.
options.better: Talk about what makes your brand special: the drinks you grew up with, made like they were at home.

options.label: Show childhood summers and home drinks. Moving, but the young may not care.

outcome.text: Your line is 'Drinks and Memories'. In 2015 your TV ads are written and spoken by a famous poet. They use the music from Malgudi Days, an old TV show, and tell stories of childhood. Sales double in a year, and in July investors put in about ₹180 crore.
Your line is 'Drinks and Memories', and your TV ads show childhood summers and drinks made at home. People feel close to the stories, and sales start growing.

options.why: Remember: sell what you stand for, not just specs. Many juice brands can talk about what's inside. Your brand was about the drinks people grew up with, and those memories made people remember you and pay more.
options.takeaway: In 2015 you sold childhood memories, not just facts about the drink. Tell people what makes your brand special.

options.label: Compare it with cola. Buyers see its value, but may focus on price.
options.outcome: Buyers start comparing your drink with colas, and your drink looks costly beside them. The ad makes people think about price instead of memories, so sales slow down.
options.why: Remember: sell what you stand for, not just specs. Price is a number people can easily compare. Your drink cost more than cola, so the ad made people think about money instead of why your brand was special.
options.better: Talk about childhood and home, and clearly say what's not inside. Don't make price the first thing people notice.
options.takeaway: In 2015 you made people compare prices. When buyers only look at price, they may choose the cheaper drink.

text.text: By 2015, Paper Boat makes up about 90% of your company's sales, and yearly sales reach about ₹24 crore. That is still small, but in July investors put in about ₹180 crore to help the company grow. Drinks no shop once sold are now sold in shops, on flights and in office canteens.

Paper Boat makes up most of your company's sales. People buy it in shops, on flights and in office canteens. A few years ago, shops didn't sell these drinks. Now people across India enjoy them, and investors want to help the company grow.
Paper Boat finds people who love its drinks in shops, on flights and in office canteens. But one less successful choice means the brand stays smaller than it could have been.

Paper Boat finally starts selling well, but a year later than it could have. By then, other brands have started copying the idea. People love your drinks, but your brand is smaller than it could have been.
Paper Boat finds people who keep buying it in a few big cities, but it doesn't look very different from other drinks. Money stays tight, and your business remains small.

collapse.title: Paper Boat runs out of money
collapse.text: You run out of money before enough people start buying your drinks. You sell your recipes to a bigger company for a small amount of money. The drinks you grew up with disappear from shops again.

fired.title: Investors take charge
fired.text: After three costly choices, your investors stop trusting your decisions and choose someone else to run the company.

realHistory: Hector Beverages sold a cheap energy drink, Tzinga. Its founders saw that old Indian drinks like aam panna were not sold in any shop. They quietly tested Paper Boat in 500 stores in February 2013, with no ads, and launched it in Delhi and Bengaluru that August in paper-look pouches that cost less than cartons. Each pack told a small childhood story, and the brand's line was 'Drinks and Memories'. For about two years it ran no TV or print ads, and people found it in shops, on flights and in office canteens. By 2015 Paper Boat was about 90% of the company's sales, yearly sales were about ₹24 crore, and investors put in about ₹180 crore.
